Infant Feeding
NRBS 3510
Summer 2026

Newborn Needs
Dietary Reference Intake (DRI, replaces RDA)
Breastfed and formula fed infants have different growth 
rates
 Both lose weight in first 3-4 days of life up to 10%
 Fluid intake is low-but NO dehydration
 Use extracellular fluid
 Begin to gain weight on day 5 of life
Breastfed infants > weight gain in first 3-4 months
After 4 months formula fed or “mixed” fed > wt gain

Fluid Requirements
 Neonatal period (1st 28 days of life) 140-160 ml/kg/day
 Infants have higher body water = 75-80% vs 60% adult
Signs and Symptoms of Neonatal Dehydration
 Any newborn with fever should be seen by MD/NP
Sunken Fontanelles Sunken Eyes Concentrated Urine
Dry chapped lips Dry oral cavity Decreased Urine 
output
Weakness Lethargy Poor Skin Turgor

Nutritional Requirements
 Basic Metabolic Rate (BMR) min energy for thermoregulation, growth, 
cellular and cardiorespiratory functions.
 Kcal: Newborns need 100-115/kcal/kg/day @ 1 Month
 Less= Risk for delayed growth and development
 Protein: Milk proteins are whey (breast) or casein (formula)
 Casein forms curds- harder to digest
 Mature breast milk = 60:40 ratio of whey to casein
 Breast milk quickly broken down= 90 minutes to digest 
 Infants should be fed 8-12 times day
 Cow’s milk has higher casein= 20:80 whey to casein
 Cow’s milk based formulas vary

Fats/Carb/Vitamin/Mineral
 Fat: 50% of their calories should be in fat
 Brain development
 Help body absorb fat-soluble vitamins
 98% of breast milk fat is triglycerides 
 Carbohydrates: 40% of calories in carbohydrates
 Lactose is primary carbohydrate in breast milk
 Helps to absorb calcium, magnesium and zinc
 Breast milk also contains glucosamines (needed for connective tissue) and 
oligosaccharides (needed for development of lactobacillus bifidus: GI flora) 
 Vitamins/Minerals/Trace Elements
 Vit A, E % K in both breast milk and formula- Vit K produced in GI tract
 No supplementation of these fat soluble vitamins- may develop toxicity
 Breast milk is low in Vit D- all infants should receive Vit D supplement.
 Cow’s milk has added Vit D. 
 Breastfed infants should receive Vit D until they begin cows milk. 
 Vitamin C & B-complex move easily from serum to breast milk
 Iron- Breast milk has less iron than formula but is more easily absorbed

Breast is Best
 The Surgeon General of the United States has called for an 
increase in the number of infants who are breastfed as the 
single most important step in improving the health of our 
future generations. 
 Exclusive breastfeeding until 6 months of age is 
recommended by:
 Continued breastfeeding until age 2 as mutually desired 
by mother and baby
 American Academy of Pediatrics
 Association of Women’s Health and Neonatal Nurses
 American College of Nurse Midwives
 American Congress of Obstetricians and Gynecologists
 American Academy of Family Practitioners
 American Public Health Association

Why Breast is Best
   Breastfed babies who are breastfed for at least 6 months are less 
likely to be overweight.
 The duration of breastfeeding also is inversely related to the risk of 
obesity.
 A reduction of 40% in the incidence of type 2 diabetes mellitus is 
reported, reflecting the long-term positive effect of breastfeeding 
on weight control and feeding self-regulation.
 80% of mothers expect to breastfeed yet only 14% are exclusively 
breastfeeding at 6 months.
 Critical periods for breastfeeding cessation are transition home 
from hospital, 6-8 weeks, transition back to work, and between 6-8 
months due to self-weaning and/or introduction of solids.

Baby Friendly Hospital Initiative
Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding
1) Have a written breastfeeding policy that is routinely communicated to all 
health care staff.
2) Train all health care staff in skills necessary to implement this policy.
3) Inform all pregnant women about the benefits and management of 
breastfeeding.
4) Help mothers initiate breastfeeding within one half-hour of birth.
5) Show mothers how to breastfeed and maintain lactation, even if they 
should be separated from their infants.
6) Give newborn infants no food or drink other than breast-milk, not even 
sips of water, unless medically indicated.
7) Practice rooming in - that is, allow mothers and infants to remain together 
24 hours a day.
8) Encourage breastfeeding on demand.
9) Give no artificial teats or pacifiers (also called dummies or soothers) to 
breastfeeding infants.
10)Foster the establishment of breastfeeding support groups and refer 
mothers to them on discharge from the hospital or clinic.
(Source: Protecting, Promoting and Supporting Breastfeeding: The Special 
Role of Maternity Services, a joint WHO/UNICEF statement published by the 
World Health Organization 2017)

Breast Milk
 Species Specific
 200 distinct components
 Bioavailable-easily absorbed
 No saturated fats
 Higher levels of nutrients for brain 
development
 Fatty acids
 Lactose-key to availability of energy
 Cystine
 Cholesterol
 Infant determines volume consumed
 Composition changes
 Health Benefits
 Decreased risk of diabetes
 Decreased obesity
 Decreased otitis-media
 Decreased URI
Formula
 Bovine or plant sources
 Missing nutrients
 DHA & ARA added (fatty 
acids) 
 Saturated Fat
 Soy formula has no lactose
 Caregiver determines feeding 
volume
 Higher rates of upper 
respiratory infections
 Higher rates of GI problems
 Potential for bacterial infections 
if not sterilized
 Higher rates of asthma, otitis-
media, diabetes

Breast vs. Formula cont’
Breast Milk
 Immunoglobulin, leukocytes
 Promotes lactobacillus
 Anti-infective properties allow for longer/safer storage
 Hypoallergenic 
 Always ready
Maternal Benefits/Other Benefits
 Faster return to pre-pregnancy weight 
 Decreased risk of breast and ovarian cancers
 Lower rates of PP depression
 Enhanced bonding
 Cost= overall savings of $400 - $1500yr
 Healthy diet/breast pump/nursing bras
Potential negatives 
 Breastfeeding at work may be difficult
 May feel embarrassed or uncomfortable
 May feel pain
 Limit birth control options – no estrogens
Formula
 Cow’s milk allergy common
 Hypoallergenic formula $$$
 No anti-infective properties
 Preparation is time consuming
 $ for formula/bottles/nipples
 Must be refrigerated
Benefits
 Available when mother is ill or on medication
 Additional maternal rest 
 Fathers can participate in feeding
 Mothers may feel more freedom
 Open birth control options

Supporting Breastfeeding
Initial Feeding- promotes bonding releases oxytocin
Begin within 1 hour of life- infant is alert and ready
Infant may be uninterested in nursing for first few days
 Late pre-term infants (35-38) may be more sleepy
 Sleepy babies may lose excessive wt. (>10%)
 Teach parents to wake infant when in “light sleep”
 Undress and check diaper (provide skin-to-skin cover dyad)
 If baby falls asleep at breast- stimulate infant
Established breastfeeding- every 1.5 to 3 hours (8-12 feedings per day)
May “cluster feed” in first few days: 5-10 feedings over 2-3 hours with 
light sleep in between
 New mothers may interpret this as “not satisfied”
 Necessary to establish/stimulate mothers milk

Latch & Position
 Position infant abdomen toward mother
 Use pillows or “boppy pillow” to support mother and 
infant
 Infant’s head is supported and guided to breast
 Illicit rooting reflex with finger or breast
 When infant’s mouth is wide-bring infant to breast with 
“chin first” angle
 Infant must take as much of areola as possible into 
mouth
Common Positions
C-hold for breast
Scissor hold of breast
Center Nipple
Rooting Reflex

Wash Hands/tops of cans  and Sterilize Storage

products 
 Use premixed=$$$ or powder mixed

heat 15 min (older babies may drink 
cold formula)
Time until Discard
 Prepared/opened-room temp-4 hour
 >79OF = 1hour 
 Prepared or liquid can-open
 Refrigerator = 24-48 hours
 Powder room temp = 1 month
Breast Milk
 Store in glass products-antibodies cling to 
plastic 
 Wash pump attachments with warm soapy 
water let air dry
 Thaw frozen milk in warm tap water for 15 
minutes or overnight in fridge
Time until Discard
 Fresh Milk-room temp-4 hour
 >79OF = 1hour 
  Fresh Milk-cooler pack=59OF = 24 hrs
 Fresh Milk in fridge (38O)=8 days
 Fresh Milk in freezer=3 months
 Thawed Milk in fridge=24 hours
 DO NOT REFREEZE!

Formula Feeding
WHO, UNICEF, AAP, AWHONN, ACNM, ACOG recognize that there are medically 
acceptable reasons to supplement:
Maternal Indications for Formula Supplementation 
 Maternal HIV infection
 Maternal Herpes Simplex Virus Type-1 (HSV-1) infection with active lesions on 
the breasts
 Cytotoxic chemotherapy
 Hepatitis-B infection (infants should receive Hepatitis B vaccine within 48hours of 
birth)
 Maternal exposure to radioactive iodine 131
 Excessive use of topical iodine or iodophors in open wounds
 Hepatitis C
 Substance use of stimulants such as cocaine, amphetamines, alcohol or ecstasy 
 Substance use of sedatives such as alcohol, opioids, cannabis or 
benzodiazepines

Supplementation
Infant Indications for Avoidance of Human Breast Milk and Supplementation 
with Specialized Formula 
Galactosemia 
Phenylketonuria 
Maple syrup urine disease 
Infant Indications for Primary Breastfeeding with Addition of Non-Human Milk 
Supplementation 
 
Preterm infants born at less than 32 weeks gestation 
Very low birth weight infants (less than 1500 grams)
Infants who are at increased risk for hypoglycemia (hypoxic stress during 
birth, infants of diabetic mothers) and whose blood glucose has not 
responded to breastfeeding

Formula Feeding Education
 Safe handling and preparation
 Avoid air intake-position 45o angle
 NEVER PROP A BOTTLE
 Only breastmilk or formula in bottle unless otherwise directed by physician
 Inadequate feeding practices associated with bottle feeding of infant 
formula or use of bottle feeding as a methods to soothe infants can 
contribute to greater than needed intake.
 It is not uncommon for mothers add cereal to the bottle in the belief that 
doing so will help the infant sleep longer.
 A substantial number of families introduce solids early especially if they 
perceive the infant as fussy.
 Inattention to a child’s hunger and satiety cues has been associated with 
infant overfeeding.
